title: Minimizing Lagrange Interpolation Basis Polynomial Integrals
description: For points x₁,...,xₙ ∈ [-1,1], what is the minimum of ∫ Σ |l_k(x)|² dx over all Lagrange basis configurations? Conjecture: min I = 2 - (1+o(1))/n. OPEN problem.

meta.author: Erdős, Szabados, Varma, Vértesi
meta.assumptions: 1 axiom: erdos_1131_conjecture (OPEN). 2 sorries: chebyshev_interp (Lagrange interpolation exactness for Chebyshev polynomials — needs polynomial uniqueness argument), chebyshev_sq_expansion (DCT Parseval identity — needs chebyshev_interp + bilinear expansion). Previously sorry lemmas now fully proved: dct_offdiag, integral_cos_substitution, integral_chebyshev_sq, chebyshev_integral_trace.

overview.historicalContext: This problem has roots in Fejér's 1932 work on optimal interpolation. Fejér proved that the zeros of the Legendre polynomial P_n minimize the maximum of the Lebesgue function Λ_n(x) = Σ|l_k(x)| over [-1,1]. Erdős naturally asked whether Legendre nodes also minimize the L² integral I = ∫Σ|l_k(x)|² dx. Szabados (1966, Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar.) disproved this for n > 3, showing that slightly perturbed nodes give a smaller integral. Erdős then conjectured min I = 2 - (1+o(1))/n. The best bounds are due to Erdős, Szabados, Varma, and Vértesi (1994, Studia Sci. Math. Hungar.): they proved 2 - O((log n)²/n) ≤ min I ≤ 2 - 2/(2n-1). The upper bound comes from Legendre nodes (I = 2 - 2/(2n-1) for P_n zeros), while the lower bound uses the partition of unity and Cauchy-Schwarz. Turetskii (1940) initiated the study of Lebesgue constants for specific node systems, and Kilgore-de Boor-Pinkus (1978) proved the existence of optimal L∞ interpolation nodes — the L² analog remains open.
overview.problemStatement: For x₁,...,xₙ ∈ [-1,1], the Lagrange basis polynomials l_k(x) satisfy l_k(x_k)=1 and l_k(x_j)=0 for j≠k. Find the minimum of I = ∫_{-1}^{1} Σ_k |l_k(x)|² dx. Is min I = 2 - (1+o(1))/n?
overview.text: A formalization of Erdős Problem #1131 on minimizing Lagrange interpolation basis polynomial integrals. Defines `NodeConfig n` (points in $[-1,1]$), Lagrange basis polynomials $l_k(x) = \prod_{i \neq k} (x - x_i)/(x_k - x_i)$, and the objective $I = \int_{-1}^{1} \sum_k l_k(x)^2\,dx$. Proves $l_k(x_j) = \delta_{kj}$ (interpolation), partition of unity $\sum l_k = 1$, the Cauchy-Schwarz lower bound $I \geq 2/n$, the identity $I = \int \sum l_k^2 = 2 - \int \sum_{j \neq k} l_j l_k$, and the equidistant upper bound $I_{\text{equi}} \leq 2 + O(\log n / n)$. Axiomatizes the Chebyshev node result $I_{\text{Cheb}} = 2 - 2/n$ and Szabados's conjecture $\min I = 2 - (1+o(1))/n$.
overview.proofStrategy: The Lean formalization defines NodeConfig, AreDistinct, lagrangeBasis (as a finite product), and the objective functional I (concrete integral definition). The cardinal basis conditions l_k(x_k) = 1 and l_k(x_j) = 0 are proved theorems, as is the partition of unity via Mathlib's Lagrange.sum_basis. The Cauchy-Schwarz lower bound I ≥ 2/n is fully proved using the variance identity. Chebyshev nodes are defined and shown to be distinct; I_Cheb ≈ 2 - c/n is axiomatized. The conjecture min I = 2 - (1+o(1))/n is stated as an axiom.
keyInsights: **Partition of unity** $\sum_k l_k(x) = 1$ gives the Cauchy-Schwarz bound $I \ge 2/n$, but the true minimum is $\approx 2 - 1/n \gg 2/n$
**Fejér vs Erdős**: Legendre nodes minimize the $L^\infty$ Lebesgue function but NOT the $L^2$ integral — Szabados (1966) disproved this for $n > 3$
**Logarithmic gap**: ESVV94 proved $2 - O((\log n)^2/n) \le \min I \le 2 - 2/(2n-1)$, leaving a $(\log n)^2$ factor unresolved
**Chebyshev vs Legendre nodes**: Both give $I \approx 2 - c/n$ but with different constants — neither is optimal for the $L^2$ problem
**Gram matrix trace**: $I = \operatorname{tr}(G)$ where $G_{jk} = \int l_j l_k \, dx$ connects the problem to spectral theory of interpolation operators

sections.title: Module Documentation
sections.summary: Module docstring summarizing Erdős Problem #1131 on minimizing $\int \sum |l_k(x)|^2\,dx$ over node configurations in $[-1,1]$. Lists all proved theorems (interpolation, orthogonality, partition of unity, Cauchy-Schwarz bound, Chebyshev node properties, exact integral formula). Imports Mathlib and opens `MeasureTheory` namespace.

sections.title: Part I: Definitions
sections.summary: Defines `NodeConfig n` (nodes in $[-1,1]$), `AreDistinct` (pairwise distinct nodes), the Lagrange basis polynomial $l_k(x)$ as a finite product over `Finset.filter`, and the objective functional `lagrangeIntegral` as the interval integral $\int_{-1}^{1} \sum_k l_k(x)^2\,dx$.
sections.mathContext: $l_k(x) = \prod_{i \ne k} \frac{x - x_i}{x_k - x_i}$, $\quad I = \int_{-1}^{1} \sum_{k=1}^{n} l_k(x)^2 \, dx$.

sections.title: Part II: Basic Properties (All Proved)
sections.summary: Four fully proved theorems: `lagrangeBasis_self` ($l_k(x_k) = 1$ by cancellation of each factor), `lagrangeBasis_other` ($l_k(x_j) = 0$ for $j \ne k$ via the zero factor), `lagrangeBasis_eq_eval_basis` (connects to Mathlib's `Lagrange.basis` by rewriting `Polynomial.eval_prod`), and `partition_of_unity` ($\sum_k l_k(x) = 1$ via `Lagrange.sum_basis` with injectivity of distinct nodes).
sections.mathContext: $l_k(x_j) = \delta_{kj}$ (Kronecker delta). Partition of unity: $\sum_{k=1}^{n} l_k(x) = 1$ for all $x$.

sections.title: Cauchy-Schwarz Lower Bound (Proved)
sections.summary: Two proved theorems establishing the universal lower bound. `sum_sq_lagrangeBasis_ge`: pointwise $\sum l_k(x)^2 \ge 1/n$ proved via the variance identity $\sum(l_k - 1/n)^2 = \sum l_k^2 - 1/n \ge 0$, expanding the square and using `partition_of_unity`. `lagrangeIntegral_lower_bound`: $I \ge 2/n$ by integral monotonicity, rewriting $2/n = \int_{-1}^{1}(1/n)\,dx$ and applying `intervalIntegral.integral_nonneg`. Includes a note that no general upper bound exists (counterexample: $n=2$, nodes at $0$ and $\delta$ give $I \to \infty$ as $\delta \to 0$).
sections.mathContext: Cauchy-Schwarz: $(\sum l_k)^2 \le n \sum l_k^2$. Since $\sum l_k = 1$: $\sum l_k^2 \ge 1/n$, hence $I \ge 2/n$.

sections.title: Part III: Chebyshev Node Definitions and Distinctness
sections.summary: Defines `chebyshevNodes n` as $x_k = \cos((2k+1)\pi/(2n))$ (roots of $T_n$). `chebyshevNodes_in_range`: nodes lie in $[-1,1]$ since $\cos$ maps to $[-1,1]$. `chebyshevNodes_distinct`: proved by showing arguments $\theta_k \in [0,\pi]$ are strictly increasing and $\cos$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, using `Real.strictAntiOn_cos.injOn`.
sections.mathContext: Chebyshev nodes of the first kind: $x_k = \cos\frac{(2k+1)\pi}{2n}$, $k = 0,\ldots,n-1$. These are zeros of $T_n(x)$.

sections.title: Part III.5: Chebyshev Integral Exact Value (Plan)
sections.summary: Detailed proof plan for the exact Chebyshev integral $I_{\text{Cheb}}(n) = 2 - 2(n-1)/(n(2n-1))$. Outlines five steps: (1) discrete cosine vanishing $\sum_k \cos(r\theta_k) = 0$ for $0 < r < 2n$, (2) DCT orthogonality, (3) Chebyshev expansion of $\sum l_k^2$, (4) integration $\int_{-1}^{1} T_j(x)^2\,dx = 1 - 1/(4j^2-1)$, and (5) telescoping partial fraction sum.

sections.title: Trigonometric Identities and Discrete Cosine Vanishing
sections.summary: Foundational trigonometric lemmas: `two_sin_mul_cos` (product-to-sum $2\sin a\cos b = \sin(a+b)+\sin(a-b)$), `sin_nat_mul_pi` ($\sin(m\pi)=0$ by induction), and the key `discrete_cosine_vanishing`: $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\cos(r\theta_k)=0$ for $0<r<2n$, proved by Abel summation — multiplying by $2\sin(r\pi/(2n))$, applying product-to-sum to get a telescoping sum via `Finset.sum_range_sub`, evaluating to $\sin(r\pi)-\sin(0)=0$.
sections.mathContext: Discrete cosine vanishing: $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \cos\!\left(\frac{r(2k+1)\pi}{2n}\right) = 0$ for $0 < r < 2n$. Proof: Abel summation with $2\sin\alpha\cos\beta = \sin(\alpha+\beta)+\sin(\alpha-\beta)$.

sections.title: Telescoping Partial Fraction Sum (Proved)
sections.summary: Fully proved `partial_fraction_sum`: $\sum_{j=0}^{m-1} \frac{1}{4(j+1)^2-1} = \frac{m}{2m+1}$, by induction on $m$. The inductive step uses `Finset.sum_range_succ`, `field_simp`, and `ring` to close the algebraic identity. This telescoping sum arises from partial fractions $\frac{1}{(2j+1)(2j+3)} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2j+1}-\frac{1}{2j+3}\right)$.

sections.title: Integration and Substitution Lemmas
sections.summary: Six fully proved lemmas for evaluating $\int_{-1}^{1} T_j(x)^2\,dx$: `two_cos_mul_sin` (product-to-sum), `integral_sin_mul` ($\int_0^\pi \sin(k\theta)\,d\theta$ by FTC with antiderivative $-\cos(k\theta)/k$), `cos_nat_mul_pi` ($\cos(m\pi)=(-1)^m$ by induction), `integral_cos_mul_sin` ($\int_0^\pi \cos(2j\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta = -2/(4j^2-1)$ via product-to-sum decomposition), `integral_cos_substitution` (change of variables $x=\cos\theta$ via `integral_comp_mul_deriv`), and `integral_chebyshev_sq` ($\int_{-1}^{1} T_j(x)^2\,dx = 1-1/(4j^2-1)$ combining substitution with cos² identity).
sections.mathContext: $\int_0^\pi \sin(k\theta)\,d\theta = \frac{1-\cos(k\pi)}{k}$. Change of variables: $\int_{-1}^{1} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta$. $\int_{-1}^{1} T_j(x)^2\,dx = 1 - \frac{1}{4j^2-1}$.

sections.title: DCT Orthogonality Infrastructure
sections.summary: Discrete Cosine Transform orthogonality at Chebyshev angles, forming the backbone of the Chebyshev expansion. `two_cos_mul_cos` (product-to-sum for cosines, proved). `frequency_abel_sum`: Abel summation identity $2\sin\beta\sum\cos(2j\beta)=(1-(-1)^s)\sin\beta$ using telescoping (proved). `frequency_cosine_sum_even`/`_odd`: frequency sums equal 0 (even $s$) or 1 (odd $s$), proved by factoring out $\sin\beta\ne 0$. `dct_diagonal`: $1+2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\cos^2(j\theta_k)=n$ (proved via `frequency_cosine_sum_odd`). `dct_offdiag`: $1+2\sum\cos(j\theta_k)\cos(j\theta_m)=0$ for $k\ne m$ (proved via product-to-sum + parity case split). `chebyshev_interp`: Lagrange interpolation exactness for Chebyshev polynomials (sorry — needs polynomial uniqueness). `chebyshev_sq_expansion`: $\sum l_k^2 = (1/n)(1+2\sum T_j^2)$ (sorry — needs chebyshev_interp + bilinear expansion).
sections.mathContext: DCT orthogonality: $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\cos(j\theta_k)\cos(m\theta_k)=\frac{1}{2}\delta_{jm}$ for $1\le j,m\le n-1$, where $\theta_k=\frac{(2k+1)\pi}{2n}$. Chebyshev expansion: $\sum_k l_k(x)^2=\frac{1}{n}\bigl(1+2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}T_j(x)^2\bigr)$.

sections.title: Chebyshev Integral: Exact Value and Estimates
sections.summary: Four fully proved theorems on the Chebyshev integral. `chebyshev_integral_trace`: trace formula $I = (1/n)(2n - 2\sum 1/(4j^2-1))$, proved by combining `chebyshev_sq_expansion` with `integral_chebyshev_sq`. `chebyshev_integral_exact`: $I = 2 - 2(n-1)/(n(2n-1))$, proved by combining the trace formula with `partial_fraction_sum`. `chebyshev_integral_lt_two`: $I < 2$ since the correction term is positive. `chebyshev_integral_estimate`: $\exists c>0$ with $|I-(2-c/n)|\le c/n^2$, proved by taking $c = n(2-I)$.

sections.title: Part IV: The Conjecture (OPEN)
sections.summary: Defines `minLagrangeIntegral n` as $\inf\{I(\mathbf{x}) : \mathbf{x} \in [-1,1]^n\}$ using `sInf`. States the open conjecture as an axiom `erdos_1131_conjecture`: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $N_0$ such that $|\min I_n - (2 - 1/n)| \le \varepsilon/n$ for all $n \ge N_0$, encoding $\min I = 2 - (1+o(1))/n$.

sections.title: Part V: Main Theorem (Proved)
sections.summary: The main formalized result `erdos_1131`: for any $n \ge 1$ and any distinct nodes in $[-1,1]$, $I \ge 2/n$. Proved by direct application of `lagrangeIntegral_lower_bound`. This establishes the universal lower bound while the tighter asymptotic behavior remains open (axiomatized conjecture).

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #1131 asks for the minimum integral of squared Lagrange basis polynomials over [-1,1]. The problem connects interpolation theory, Lebesgue constants, and L² optimization. Known bounds: 2 - O((log n)²/n) ≤ min I ≤ 2 - 2/(2n-1), with the conjecture min I = 2 - (1+o(1))/n. Legendre nodes nearly achieve the minimum, but Szabados showed they are not optimal for n > 3. The logarithmic gap in the lower bound remains the key obstacle.
conclusion.implications: Resolving this conjecture would complete our understanding of optimal node placement in L² interpolation theory, with applications to numerical quadrature, spectral methods, and approximation theory. The distinction between L∞-optimal (Kilgore-de Boor-Pinkus) and L²-optimal nodes illuminates the geometry of polynomial spaces.
openQuestions: Is min I = 2 - (1+o(1))/n? Can the (log n)² factor in the lower bound be removed?
What node configuration achieves the minimum for each n?
Is the optimal node system unique (up to reflection)?
Does the Gram matrix G_{jk} = ∫l_j l_k dx have spectral structure that explains the minimum?
What is the L² analog of the Kilgore-de Boor-Pinkus characterization of L∞-optimal nodes?

crossReferences.relationship: The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for integrals provides the key lower bound I >= 2/n via the partition of unity sum l_k = 1
Fourier analysis connects to the spectral theory of the Gram matrix G_{jk} = int l_j l_k dx, whose trace equals I
Legendre polynomials provide the near-optimal node system for the L2 interpolation problem; their zeros achieve I = 2 - 2/(2n-1)
